wstep: This card describes the Sure-Jell (Kraft Heinz) recipe for rhubarb strawberry jam: chopped rhubarb and crushed strawberries boiled with powdered pectin and sugar, filled into sterile jars and processed in a boiling-water bath.

ostrzezenia.tekst: Do not reduce the sugar: NCHFP warns that in traditional recipes too little sugar prevents gelling and may allow yeasts and molds to grow.

sekcje.naglowek: Why this jam can be canned in a boiling-water bath
akapity: According to an FDA list, rhubarb has an approximate pH of 3.10–3.40 and strawberries of 3.00–3.90.
A US cup holds about 237 ml.
Sure-Jell uses 4 cups of prepared fruit: 2 cups of chopped or thinly sliced unpeeled rhubarb, made up with crushed strawberries; buy about 1 quart of strawberries and 1 lb (about 450 g) of rhubarb.
The recipe also uses 1 box of SURE-JELL Original pectin, 1/2 teaspoon of butter and 5 1/2 cups of sugar.
Measure the fruit and sugar exactly; do not change the proportion of rhubarb and strawberries.
NCHFP warns not to reduce the sugar in traditional recipes: too little sugar prevents gelling and may allow yeasts and molds to grow.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): sterilize the jars as NCHFP describes, as USDA requires for jams made from pectin package recipes.
NCHFP puts the empty jars right side up on the rack in a boiling-water canner and fills the canner and jars with hot (not boiling) water to 1 inch (about 2.5 cm) above the tops of the jars.
To sterilize empty jars, NCHFP boils them for 10 minutes below 1000 ft, and above that 1 minute longer for each additional thousand feet.
JarAtlas rule for metres: boil the jars for 10 minutes up to 300 m, and add 1 minute for every further 300 m or part of it.
Bring the fruit with the pectin to a full rolling boil, stir in the sugar, return to a full rolling boil and boil exactly 1 minute, stirring constantly.
Just before filling, remove and drain the hot sterilized jars one at a time.
Ladle the jam immediately into the jars, filling to within 1/4 inch (about 0.6 cm) of the tops.
Do not seal the jars with paraffin or wax: NCHFP no longer recommends paraffin or wax seals for any sweet spread, because of possible mold contamination.
Place the jars in a boiling-water canner with the water 1–2 inches above the jars, bring the water to a gentle boil and process.
Up to 1000 ft (up to 300 m) process the jars for 10 minutes.
Above 1000 ft the food may spoil if the time is not increased.

Above 1000 ft Sure-Jell adds time to these 10 minutes: add 5 minutes at 1001–3000 ft (above 300 m up to 900 m), 10 minutes at 3001–6000 ft (above 900 m up to 1800 m), 15 minutes at 6001–8000 ft (above 1800 m up to 2400 m) and 20 minutes at 8001–10000 ft (above 2400 m up to 3000 m).
Above 10000 ft (above 3000 m) Sure-Jell gives no time, so this card does not cover canning at that elevation.
The card converts feet to metres and rounds the limits down, towards the longer time: 1000 ft becomes 300 m, 3000 ft becomes 900 m and 6000 ft becomes 1800 m.
8000 ft (2438.4 m) becomes 2400 m and 10000 ft (3048 m) becomes 3000 m, so the range without a time is wider than in the source.
Shortening the time or cooling jars in cold water can also lead to spoilage.
NCHFP gives times for jams and jellies made with packaged pectin only for half-pint and pint jars; JarAtlas rule: use only these jars for this recipe.
JarAtlas rule (NCHFP does not test metric jars): a pint holds about 473 ml, so a 0.5 l jar has no tested time in this recipe; use jars of up to 473 ml.
When you take the hot jars out of the canner, do not retighten the lids or bands; this can cut through the gasket and cause seal failures.

Cool the jars at room temperature for 12 to 24 hours, then remove only the screw bands (the metal rings of two-piece lids), leaving the flat lids on the jars, and test the seal: press the middle of the lid, and if it springs up when you release it, the jar is not sealed.

NCHFP calls Mason-type canning jars with self-sealing two-piece lids (a flat lid and a screw band) the best choice, and this seal test and the method on this card assume them; NCHFP does not recommend other commercial jars whose mouths cannot be sealed with two-piece canning lids for canning any food at home.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): use this card only with jars that take two-piece canning lids; it gives no method for twist-off jars or jars with glass lids, so do not use them for this recipe.
A sealed lid is concave, curved down slightly in the centre; if the centre is flat or bulging, the jar may not be sealed.
If a jar has not sealed at this check, keep it in the refrigerator and eat it within several days.

Store sealed jars in a clean, cool, dark, dry place, not above 95 °F (35 °C) and not near hot pipes, a stove or a furnace, in an uninsulated attic or in direct sunlight; in such conditions the food may spoil.

Store sealed jars in a cool, dark, dry place at 50–70 °F (about 10–21 °C) and use them within a year: NCHFP says jams and jellies made from a tested recipe and processed for the recommended time keep their best quality for up to a year.
Keep opened jam in the refrigerator at 40 °F (about 4 °C) or lower.
Regular full-sugar cooked jams made with added pectin, like this one, are best kept in the refrigerator for 1 month after opening.
Opening the jar often or leaving it out at room temperature for long periods shortens this time; you can spoon the amount you need into a bowl and put the jar back in the refrigerator quickly.
Keep the opened jar in the refrigerator until it is used up.
Before using a stored jar, check that the lid is tight and holds a vacuum: a good seal has a concave centre.
Look for streaks of dried food running from the top of the jar, rising air bubbles and unnatural colour.
When opening the jar, check for an unnatural smell, spurting liquid and cotton-like mould on the food or under the lid.
Do not taste food from a jar with an unsealed lid or with signs of spoilage.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): throw out such a jar.
Discard jam with mold on it; USDA and microbiologists advise against scooping out the mold and eating the rest.
Check an opened jar regularly for signs of spoilage such as mold, yeast or an off odor, including a fermented, yeasty or alcohol smell; if you find any, throw out the whole jar.
